topic: Public Service Values, Ethics & Probity in Governance

items.title: Values & Ethics in Public Administration
items.body:
## Why ethics matters in public administration

Public servants wield **discretionary power over public resources**, so their conduct must be anchored in values, not just rules. Ethics supplies the *why*; law supplies the *what*.

## Core civil-service values

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Integrity | Consistency of conduct with declared values; probity |
| Impartiality | Decisions on merit, without bias, fear or favour |
| Political neutrality | Serve any lawfully elected government; loyalty to the Constitution |
| Anonymity | Minister is accountable; the civil servant advises behind the scenes |
| Objectivity, dedication, compassion for the weak | Emphasised by the 2nd ARC and Nolan principles |

## Status & problems

- **Value erosion**: politicisation, corruption, red-tapism, nexus of politician-bureaucrat-contractor.
- **Ethical dilemmas**: conflict between rules and conscience, personal vs public interest, ends vs means, loyalty to superior vs to law.
- **Sources of ethical guidance**: (i) **laws, rules and regulations** set the outer limit; (ii) **conscience** guides where rules are silent or in conflict; supplemented by codes, precedents and constitutional morality.

## Accountability & strengthening moral values

- **Accountability types** — vertical (to citizens: elections, social audit, RTI), horizontal (to CAG, CVC, courts), political (to legislature).
- **Strengthening measures** — value-based recruitment and training (LBSNAA, MCRHRD Institute in AP), codes of ethics, whistle-blower protection, leadership by example, citizen participation.
keyPoints: Core values: integrity, impartiality, political neutrality, anonymity, objectivity and compassion.
Political neutrality = loyalty to the Constitution and to any elected government, not to a party.
Main problems: politicisation, corruption, red-tapism, value erosion.
Sources of ethical guidance: laws/rules/regulations (outer limit) + conscience (inner guide).
Accountability is vertical (citizens), horizontal (audit bodies) and political (legislature).
Moral values are strengthened through training, codes of ethics and whistle-blower protection.

items.title: Ethics in International Relations, Funding & Corporate Governance
items.body:
## Ethics in international relations

- States are expected to honour **treaties (pacta sunt servanda)**, respect **sovereignty and non-interference**, and pursue **peaceful settlement** of disputes.
- Tension between **national interest (realism)** and **universal moral values (idealism)** — e.g., human-rights concerns vs strategic ties.
- India's tradition: **Panchsheel**, non-alignment and 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' as ethical anchors.

## Ethics in funding

- **Foreign aid/funding** can carry **conditionalities** that compromise autonomy — raising ethical questions of sovereignty.
- **Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010 (FCRA)** regulates foreign contributions to associations/NGOs; **PMLA 2002** targets money laundering.
- Concerns: opaque political funding, foreign influence, and misuse of charitable funds.

## Corporate governance

- Definition: the **system of rules, practices and processes** by which a company is directed and controlled, balancing interests of **all stakeholders**.
- **Pillars**: transparency, accountability, fairness, responsibility.
- **Framework in India**: Companies Act 2013 (independent directors, audit committees, CSR), SEBI (LODR) Regulations 2015; shaped by the **Kumar Mangalam Birla, Narayana Murthy and Kotak** committees.
- Failures (e.g., Satyam scam) show how weak governance harms investors and public trust.
keyPoints: International ethics: honour treaties, respect sovereignty, peaceful dispute settlement; realism vs idealism.
FCRA 2010 regulates foreign contributions to NGOs; PMLA 2002 tackles money laundering.
Foreign aid conditionalities can raise sovereignty/ethical concerns.
Corporate governance balances the interests of all stakeholders, not just shareholders.
Pillars of corporate governance: transparency, accountability, fairness, responsibility.
Indian framework: Companies Act 2013 + SEBI (LODR) 2015; Birla, Murthy and Kotak committees.

items.title: Probity in Governance — Concept, Philosophy & Nolan Principles
items.body:
## Concept of probity

**Probity** means proven **integrity, uprightness and honesty** in the conduct of public affairs — treating public office as a **public trust**. It goes beyond mere legality to ethical rightness.

## Philosophical basis

- **Public office as trust**: authority is held for the people, not for private gain.
- **Dharma / righteousness** and the idea of *nishkama karma* (selfless duty).
- **Gandhi's seven social sins**: politics without principles; wealth without work; commerce without morality; pleasure without conscience; education without character; science without humanity; worship without sacrifice.

## Nolan's Seven Principles of Public Life (UK, 1994-95)

| # | Principle | Essence |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Selflessness | Act solely in the public interest |
| 2 | Integrity | Avoid obligations that could influence decisions |
| 3 | Objectivity | Decide impartially, on merit and evidence |
| 4 | Accountability | Submit to scrutiny |
| 5 | Openness | Act transparently |
| 6 | Honesty | Be truthful |
| 7 | Leadership | Promote and exemplify these principles |

## 2nd ARC 4th Report — 'Ethics in Governance' (2007)

- Chaired by **M. Veerappa Moily**.
- Recommended a **Code of Ethics** for ministers, legislators and civil servants; strengthening of the CVC and Lokpal; protection for whistle-blowers; partial state funding of elections; and reducing discretion to curb corruption.
keyPoints: Probity = integrity and uprightness in public affairs; public office is a public trust.
Philosophical basis: trusteeship, dharma/righteousness, and Gandhi's seven social sins.
Nolan's seven principles: selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty, leadership.
Nolan principles were framed by the UK Committee on Standards in Public Life (1994-95).
2nd ARC 4th Report 'Ethics in Governance' (2007) was chaired by Veerappa Moily.
It recommended codes of ethics, whistle-blower protection and reduced discretion.
items.source: 2nd ARC 4th Report (2007); UK Committee on Standards in Public Life

items.title: Transparency, Information Sharing & the RTI Act, 2005
items.body:
## Transparency as a probity tool

**Information sharing and transparency** deter corruption by exposing decisions to public scrutiny; secrecy is the natural ally of malpractice.

## Right to Information Act, 2005

- Replaced the **Freedom of Information Act, 2002**; flows from **Article 19(1)(a)** (speech) and **Article 21**.
- Any citizen may seek information from a **'public authority'**; reply within **30 days** (**48 hours** where life/liberty is involved).
- **Section 4** mandates **proactive (suo motu) disclosure**; **Section 8** lists exemptions (national security, cabinet papers, personal information, etc.).
- **Public Information Officers (PIOs)** handle requests; appeals go to the **First Appellate Authority**, then the **Central/State Information Commission (CIC/SIC)**.
- **2019 amendment**: empowered the Centre to fix the **tenure and salaries** of Information Commissioners (criticised as diluting independence).

## Complementary measures

- **Social audit** (mandatory under MGNREGA), **e-governance** portals, **open data**, and **DBT** enhance transparency and cut leakages.
- Balancing transparency with **privacy** and **legitimate confidentiality** is a live ethical challenge.
keyPoints: RTI Act 2005 replaced the Freedom of Information Act 2002; rooted in Articles 19(1)(a) and 21.
Information within 30 days; 48 hours where life or liberty is involved.
Section 4 requires proactive disclosure; Section 8 lists exemptions.
Appellate structure: PIO -> First Appellate Authority -> CIC/SIC.
The 2019 amendment let the Centre fix Information Commissioners' tenure and salaries.
Transparency must be balanced against privacy and legitimate confidentiality.

items.title: Codes of Conduct, Citizen's Charters & Use of Public Funds
items.body:
## Codes of ethics vs codes of conduct

| Aspect | Code of Ethics | Code of Conduct |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | Broad guiding **values** | Specific enforceable **dos-and-don'ts** |
| Example | 2nd ARC's proposed code of ethics | AIS (Conduct) Rules 1968 |

- **All India Services (Conduct) Rules, 1968** — apply to IAS/IPS/IFoS: require integrity, devotion to duty and political neutrality; restrict gifts, speculation, and unauthorised media contact.
- **AP Civil Services (Conduct) Rules, 1964** — govern Andhra Pradesh state services on similar lines.

## Citizen's Charters, work culture & service delivery

- A **Citizen's Charter** publicly declares **service standards, timelines and grievance redress**; the **Sevottam** model assesses its implementation.
- Charters improve **work culture**, **responsiveness** and **quality of service delivery** but are generally **not legally enforceable** (unlike Public Service Guarantee Acts).

## Utilisation of public funds

- Probity demands **economy, efficiency and effectiveness** ('3 Es') in spending; funds are held in trust for the public.
- Safeguards: **budgetary controls**, **CAG audit**, **Public Accounts Committee**, outcome budgeting and **social audit** against leakage and misuse.
keyPoints: Code of ethics = broad values; code of conduct = enforceable rules.
AIS (Conduct) Rules 1968 apply to IAS/IPS/IFoS; AP Civil Services (Conduct) Rules 1964 to state services.
Citizen's Charter declares service standards, timelines and grievance redress; assessed via Sevottam.
Charters are usually not legally enforceable, unlike Public Service Guarantee Acts.
Use of public funds must follow economy, efficiency and effectiveness (3 Es).
CAG audit, PAC and social audit safeguard proper utilisation of public funds.
items.source: AIS (Conduct) Rules 1968; AP Civil Services (Conduct) Rules 1964; DARPG Sevottam

items.title: Challenges of Corruption & the Anti-Corruption Architecture
items.body:
## Corruption: forms and costs

- Forms: **bribery, nepotism, favouritism, embezzlement, extortion, collusion** and 'speed money'.
- Costs: erodes trust, distorts development, hurts the poor most, and undermines the rule of law.

## Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 & 2018 amendment

- The **PC Act, 1988** (31 sections) is the principal anti-bribery law; cases are tried by designated **Special Judges**.
- The **PC (Amendment) Act, 2018** (in force **26 July 2018**):
  - made **bribe-giving a distinct offence** and introduced **'undue advantage'**;
  - made **commercial organisations** liable (Section 9);
  - required **prior approval (Section 17A)** to investigate official decisions of public servants;
  - set a **time-bound trial** (endeavour to conclude within two years); aligned the law with the **UN Convention against Corruption**.

## Institutional framework

| Body | Basis | Role |
|---|---|---|
| **Lokpal** | Lokpal & Lokayuktas Act, 2013 | National ombudsman; chairperson + up to 8 members (half judicial); covers PM (with safeguards), MPs, central Group A-D |
| **Lokayukta** | State Acts (AP Lokayukta Act, 1983) | State-level ombudsman |
| **CVC** | CVC Act, 2003 (Santhanam Committee, 1964) | Apex integrity/vigilance body; superintendence over CBI in PC Act cases |
| **CBI** | DSPE Act, 1946 | Premier investigating agency |
| **AP ACB** | State agency | Investigates PC Act offences in Andhra Pradesh |

- Reform ideas (2nd ARC): reduce discretion, protect whistle-blowers, ensure transparency, and speed up prosecution.
keyPoints: PC Act 1988 is the principal anti-bribery law; tried by Special Judges.
PC (Amendment) Act 2018 (26 July 2018) made bribe-giving a distinct offence and defined 'undue advantage'.
The 2018 amendment added Section 17A prior approval and a two-year time-bound trial.
Lokpal (2013 Act): chairperson + up to 8 members, half judicial; covers PM with safeguards, MPs and Group A-D.
CVC is statutory under the CVC Act 2003, traced to the Santhanam Committee (1964).
AP ACB investigates PC Act cases in Andhra Pradesh; Lokayukta is the state ombudsman (AP Act, 1983).
items.source: PC Act 1988 & Amendment 2018; Lokpal & Lokayuktas Act 2013; CVC Act 2003
